lessons.title: African nationalism and decolonisation
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board, Advanced Level History syllabus (Upper Sixth) — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Explain the internal and external causes of decolonisation
Compare peaceful and violent routes to independence
Place the independence of Ghana, Algeria and southern Africa in sequence
reviewNotes: Verify: Ghana 6 March 1957; ‘Year of Africa’ 1960 — number of states (about 17); Algeria 1962; Portuguese colonies 1975; Zimbabwe 1980; Namibia 1990; South Africa 1994; Atlantic Charter 1941.
Check which case studies the syllabus requires.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Causes
blocks.md: **Internal:** educated elites, nationalist parties and newspapers, growing towns and trade unions, ex-servicemen who fought in the Second World War, and resentment of forced labour, taxes and discrimination. **External:** the weakening of Britain and France by the war, the Atlantic Charter (1941) and its language of self-determination, the stance of the UN, the USA and the USSR, and the independence of India and other Asian countries from 1947.

blocks.title: Routes to independence
blocks.md: Many colonies became independent by **negotiation and elections**, led by parties such as Nkrumah’s in the Gold Coast, which became **Ghana in 1957**, the first sub-Saharan colony to gain independence from Britain. In **1960**, often called the ‘Year of Africa’, about seventeen states became independent, including Cameroon (French Cameroun), Nigeria, Senegal and the Congo.

blocks.caption: Decolonisation milestones in Africa.
blocks.alt: Timeline from 1945 to 1995 with Ghana 1957, the Year of Africa 1960, Algeria 1962, Angola and Mozambique 1975, Zimbabwe 1980 and South Africa 1994.

blocks.title: Armed struggles
blocks.md: Where settlers or colonial governments resisted, independence involved conflict: the **Algerian war** (1954–62) ended with independence in 1962; Portuguese colonies such as Angola and Mozambique became independent in **1975** after wars; Zimbabwe in **1980**; Namibia in **1990**; in South Africa apartheid ended with the first multiracial elections in **1994**.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Decolonisation was not simply ‘given’: African movements pushed for it.
- ‘Peaceful’ does not mean there was no repression or suffering in the earlier years.
- Do not give 1960 as the independence date of every African state: look up each one.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Internal or external?
blocks.statement: Classify these causes: (a) formation of a nationalist party, (b) the Atlantic Charter, (c) returning soldiers’ demands.
steps: (b) A statement by Britain and the USA: external.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Compare Ghana and Algeria
blocks.statement: Briefly compare how Ghana and Algeria gained independence.
steps: Ghana: political campaigns and elections; independence by agreement in 1957.
Algeria: a long armed struggle (1954–62) against a state that treated the territory as part of France.
Both show the effect of nationalist organisation, but circumstances differed.

lessons.title: Independence and reunification of Cameroon (general outline)
lessons.programRef: Cameroon GCE Board, Advanced Level History syllabus (Upper Sixth) — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Outline the road to independence of French Cameroun and the British Cameroons
Describe the 1961 plebiscites and the federation
reviewNotes: Verify: trusteeship 1946; 1 Jan 1960; Nigeria 1 Oct 1960; plebiscites 11 Feb 1961 (date often given); Foumban talks July 1961; 1 Oct 1961 federation; 20 May 1972 referendum; 1984 name change.
Politically sensitive: keep neutral and follow the official syllabus; the plebiscite options and later debates must be presented as the syllabus requires.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: French Cameroun
blocks.md: French Cameroun was a UN trust territory from 1946. Political movements demanded autonomy, reunification and independence, among them the Union des Populations du Cameroun (UPC, founded in 1948). Self-government was introduced in stages in the 1950s. **French Cameroun became independent on 1 January 1960** as the Republic of Cameroun, with Ahmadou Ahidjo as first president.

blocks.title: British Cameroons
blocks.md: Nigeria became independent on **1 October 1960**. The UN organised **plebiscites in the British Cameroons in February 1961**. The northern part (**Northern Cameroons**) voted to join Nigeria. The southern part (**Southern Cameroons**) voted to join the Republic of Cameroun. Constitutional discussions in Foumban in July 1961 followed.

blocks.caption: Key dates in Cameroon’s unification and constitutional history.
blocks.alt: Timeline from 1946 to 1984 with trusteeship, independence of French Cameroun, plebiscites and federation, unitary state and name change.

blocks.title: Federation and later changes
blocks.md: The **Federal Republic of Cameroon** was created on **1 October 1961**, with two federated states, East and West Cameroon. After a referendum in **May 1972** the federation became a unitary state, the **United Republic of Cameroon**. In **1984** the name became the **Republic of Cameroon**. Different views exist today about some of these arrangements; students should state facts and attribute opinions.

blocks.title: Neutral writing
blocks.md:
- Use dates and documented decisions; attribute views (‘supporters argued…’).
- Do not confuse independence of French Cameroun (1960) with the union of 1961.
- The plebiscite concerned the British-administered territory only.
- Avoid emotive language: describe, explain, assess.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Sequence
blocks.statement: Put in order: plebiscites, independence of French Cameroun, federation, UN trusteeship, unitary state.
steps: French Cameroun became independent on 1 January 1960.
Plebiscites were held in February 1961 and the federation was created in October 1961.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Plebiscite results explained
blocks.statement: Explain the outcome of the 1961 plebiscites in general terms.
steps: Voters in Northern Cameroons chose to join Nigeria.
Voters in Southern Cameroons chose to join the Republic of Cameroun.
The choices reflected differing links, interests and political campaigns in each area.
blocks.answer: A divided result: north to Nigeria, south to Cameroun.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Assess the importance of the Second World War as a cause of decolonisation in Africa.
exercises.model: The war weakened Britain and France financially and militarily, so they were less able to hold colonies. African soldiers returned with new ideas and expectations, wartime demand and inflation fuelled grievances, and statements like the Atlantic Charter raised hopes. But nationalism already existed and the USA, the USSR and the UN also pushed for change. The war was a major but not the only cause.

exercises.prompt: Explain why the UN held plebiscites in the British Cameroons.
exercises.model: The territory was a UN trust territory, so the UN, as supervising body, organised the vote to let the inhabitants decide their future. Trusteeship required that inhabitants be consulted, and the plebiscites were a way to choose between the options put forward.
exercises.rubric: Trust territory (1); supervision (1); inhabitants’ consent (1); options (1).
exercises.explanation: The territory was a UN trust territory, so the UN, as supervising body, organised the vote to let the inhabitants decide their future. Trusteeship required that inhabitants be consulted, and the plebiscites were a way to choose between the options put forward.
